p.hi: Interview with Mr. George Johnson, Mound Bayou, Mississippi, September 1941

div.p: Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Oh, ah, you say you, you in AME? [African Methodist Episcopal Church]
Mr. George Johnson: AME, yes, sir.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Do you remember how you got religion down there on the ah, plantation?

Mr. George Johnson: Oh, lord, yes indeed, yeah, yeah, indeed. We just got, just got converted just, right in daytime. Right in the daytime. God spoke peace to our soul, that's in the daytime. Noontime. It's just noontime. Cause it's called noontime. Eleven o'clock. Yes, sir. Ain't no question about it. We didn't have, I didn't go to no ??? . Just got, got blessed right ??? come home to and told mom about it.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Mhmm.
Mr. George Johnson: And they saw me carried me on to church. And took me to church that same day, same night.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Well, were they running a [protracted (?)] meeting?
Mr. George Johnson: Yes, sir. Yes, sir. Right on Hurricane.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Mhmm.
Mr. George Johnson: Right on Hurricane. Right on Jeff Davis plantation.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Ah do,do you remember who the preacher was?
Mr. George Johnson: Oh, I know his name better than I know my own name: O. A. Douglass.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: O. A. Douglass?
Mr. George Johnson: O. A. Douglass, pastor our church.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Wa, wa, was he a good, good preacher?
Mr. George Johnson: Yes, sir. Yes, sir. Yes, sir.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Ah wha, what kind of songs did they sing in the church then?

Mr. George Johnson: Now, ah, well they sing songs like they sing now. Now let me tell you a song we used to sing when I was a boy: Mercy Seat, the calm and easy Mercy Seat. See. We sang that song. We sang that song down there when I was a little boy. [sings]

There is a calm, Oh, sure to be.
It's underneath the Mercy Seat.
Oh, Mercy Seat.
Oh, Mercy Seat.
Calm to be, Oh, Mercy Seat.
There is a calm, Oh, sure to be.
Around a calm, Oh, Mercy Seat.
Mr. George Johnson: That's one of our favorite songs.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Mhmm.
Mr. George Johnson: Yes, sir right in church. And all the women shout: ‘My Lord, oh mercy.’
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: [laughter]
Mr. George Johnson: Yes, sir.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Did they have these things in this church then that they called the shouts?
Mr. George Johnson: Shouts? Yes, sir. Yes, sir. They shout without end.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Well, I don't mean when they, when they ju, ju, jump up and shout, but these, these kind of singing they called the shouts, then?
Mr. George Johnson: No, sir. I don't think we did. No, sir. Not in my day.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Di, di, di, did they have any Baptist on your plantation?
Mr. George Johnson: Yes, sir. We had plenty Baptist. Plenty Baptist. Main church we had there Baptist Church.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Di,di,did they do any different singing and things from what you all did?
Mr. George Johnson: Mighty little. Mighty little.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: You all sang about the same things they did?

Mr. George Johnson: Yes, sir. They all was [something brushes against the microphone] well reckon they Christianized, you understand, under the ??? of ah, they pastor and our pastor, you understand, they all sang together. They mixed. You couldn't hardly find tell the difference, you know. Cause they all mixed together. Go to one church. Go to the other, see.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Mhmm.
Mr. George Johnson: They all ??? . They all Christianized. Yes, sir. All Christianized.

Charles S. Johnson: Well ah, di,di,did you all have any ah, did, did, did, did,did you remember any of the Negroes singing in the fields? Any s- songs out there? Any songs they liked to sing when they were out in the fields?
Mr. George Johnson: In the fields? [steam engine snorts] I hear them, I used hear them singing Old Black Joe, in the fields.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: You did?
[steam engine creeps forward tolling its bell]
Mr. George Johnson: Yes, sir. When I was quite a boy I sing, Old Black Joe. Remember that song used to sing:

Gone am the days
when my heart was young and gay.

Gone am the friend
from a cotton field away.

Gone from this world
to a better world I know.
I ??? a voice a calling, Old Black Joe.

I am coming
keep a coming.
From ???
I am a ??? a voice a calling, Old Black Joe.
[steam engine muscles down the tracks]
Mr. George Johnson: Yeah, you see that's how men sing out in the field. Yes, sir.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Di, di, di, did they sing any reels? [the train pushes through with a head of steam]

Mr. George Johnson: Well, I don't know that much. I ain't hear but ??? . Most things I hear them, I hear at down pretty far from where I lived, you understand. Right around here, they didn't sing no tough songs, you understand, around, near the house. You understand. See cause still Missile Hill.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Still Missile Hill tough song.
Mr. George Johnson: Yeah, Missile Hill. Yes tough song, they wouldn't sing that around the house.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Mhmm
Mr. George Johnson: But I always down in master Jeff's yard, you understand. Down in Grandpa's shop. And ah, they wouldn't. ??? mighty nice down there ??? . Yes, sir.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Well, did you ah, did the, who, when'd you first hear the blues?
Mr. George Johnson: After I come up here.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: After you came up here to Mound Bayou?
Mr. George Johnson: Yes. Yes, sir. Yes, sir.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Well, what do you think about the blues? Do you think they're good music, eh?
Mr. George Johnson: Well, I don't, I don't like it.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: You don't like the blues?
Mr. George Johnson: Don't like the blues. It's too wild for me. I'm scared of it.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: It's too wild?
Mr. George Johnson: Too wild. Hear it when come up here. Yes, sir. Yes, sir.
[steam engine whistles]
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Well, in the song, in the ah, in the dances that that you all had up here, you all didn't play any of that kind of music for your dances?

Mr. George Johnson: No, sir. No, sir. No sir. We played. We played, now this here, we play up here now, this Ragtime stuff they play now, why, that's today's stuff, you understand. That's modern dance, you understand. See.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Mhmm.
Mr. George Johnson: Now we be dancing fourteen on a set.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Mhmm.
Mr. George Johnson: Yeah, four over there. Four over there. Four here and four there. And they all dance. They call Swing, you understand. Part as you swing.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Mhmm.

Mr. George Johnson: Meet your partners, like that, you understand. See. Part as you swing. Dance to your partner. Dance to your right. Dance to your left. Then on to your partner. Then on to the other fellow, you understand, see.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Mhmm.

Mr. George Johnson: And then get bring pull in to your partner. Your partner pull you back. Then pull back to your partner again. Then half swing around. Half swing around. Till you got to the bar then point her to the bar.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Mhmm.
Mr. George Johnson: That, that's the dance we had then. Yes, sir.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Did you ever play any for the white people's dances?
Mr. George Johnson: Down there?
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Mhmm.
Mr. George Johnson: Played music. Brass band for them.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: That's what I mean.
Mr. George Johnson: Yes, sir. Played string band for white folks. Brass band.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Wha, what, what kind of, what kind of music di, di, did they have? They have the same you had, or did they have different songs you played for them?

Mr. George Johnson: Naw, they we, we, we played just the string band. Me and the brass band played for white folk. They'd have a big outing, you understand. In their lawn. We played music for them, you understand. Brass band music, you know.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Mhmm.
Mr. George Johnson: They'd have people up there dancing. They-they-they, they didn't ??? somebody wouldn't have a dance like the way we have. They just dance, you understand, in their way.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Mhmm.
Mr. George Johnson: But we played that brass band music, you understand. You see.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Mhmm.
Mr. George Johnson: Yes, sir. We played that square front of Joe Davis' house. Right in the shade. Right in the great big shade. Right in Joe Davis' ya, ya, yard. Yard big as the railroad over there.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Mhmm.
Mr. George Johnson: Yes, sir. Like, master Jeff's yard was. Yes, sir.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Well ah, you didn't like these songs like ah, Joe Turner: Make Me A Pallet On the Floor?
Mr. George Johnson: No, sir. I didn't like those kind things. No, sir. No, sir. I hear a guy that come up here. Yes, sir.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Ah what year was that? Ah wha, wha, what year did you first hear there? About what time was it—
Mr. George Johnson: Oh, been about fifty-years ago.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Mhmm.
Mr. George Johnson: Since I been here.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Mhmm.
Mr. George Johnson: I been here fifty-four years, going on fifty-five.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Mhmm.
Mr. George Johnson: I didn't know [anything (?)] about it since I come up here.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Mhmm.
Mr. George Johnson: Yes, sir. ??? . They got the lake stuff, come up out of the lake Negro, you understand, see. And he wild. He just say anything.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: [laugh] Say anything.

Mr. George Johnson: Say anything. He wild. Don't have any culture. Hard to educate, educate him in a way, but in a way he ain't educated. But what he got to do is learn to get his self culture, he won't think he's a little [stuups (?)].
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Mhmm.

Mr. George Johnson: Sure he'll do it. Get his self culture. He won't get him a little [schooling (?)]. He won't do it. Some fellows say, “Well, he'll do so and so,” but he ain't used to doing that. Christ said, ‘Lift me up.’ Say, ‘If I am lifted it's all men.’ Lift them up. That's all men can lift himself up. [taps walking stick] That' he got do. This man don't want to do his self like he ain't much. He going be just down there all, down there all the time. He don't care to being raggedy no, no other men. ??? .
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Ah did, did, did they ever sing the hallee, the hallees, the jubilee songs in the AME Church? They sing a lot of them, used to sing a lot of them in the Baptist Church.
Mr. George Johnson: Yeah, yeah, yeah they did sing them sometime. Sing them. They sing them. They sing them.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Did you like them?
Mr. George Johnson: Yes. Yes. Yes, they were all, they were all, all, they all right.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Mhmm.
Mr. George Johnson: We had a preacher in our church, ??? . His name, S. C. Johnson. He could sing world, he could sing how a goat sing. Hollering.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Mhmm.
Mr. George Johnson: He could sing without end. He just sing. Then he could preach.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Mhmm.

Mr. George Johnson: He could preach. He had a song he used to sing. Say, “The apostle of God, whose salvation he give onto them who love them.” His son, he would, he, he, his son ??? . [Sing that ??? (?)]. I remember that song:

Hallelujah it's done.
I believe on the son.
I am saved by the blood of the crucified one.
Though the pathway be lonely.
And dangerous truth.

Surely Jesus is able to carry me through.
Hallelujah it is done.
I believe on the son.
I am saved by the blood of the crucified one.
Mr. George Johnson: That man could sing that song.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Mhmm.
Mr. George Johnson: He could sing it. The whole church [catch it (?)], understand. You see.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Mhmm.
Mr. George Johnson: Yes, sir.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Well ah, ah, how how do you like the Dr. Watts songs, these long meter things?
Mr. George Johnson: Long meters? Well, I didn't care much about them. But I got to hear them. But I never, I never could sing them.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Never could sing them.

Mr. George Johnson: Never could sing them. No, sir. Yeah, I heard Dr. Watts' songs lots of times, never could sing them. I had a quick ??? in, in speech. And singing and all that kind of stuff. I learned quick, you understand.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Mhmm.
Mr. George Johnson: Then I'm part, I'm Creole.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Mhmm.
Mr. George Johnson: I'm part Creole. My father was [Virginian (?)] but my mother was from down in Louisiana. Down in, on, on,on,in a cane farm.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Mhmm.

Mr. George Johnson: Place the other side of a New, part of New Orleans there. New Orleans there. Born on the Louisiana side. I can't remember that place now. Her and her brother and my aunty, but my father's from Richmond. My father and my grandfather are from Richmond. My father's brother, uncle Charlie.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Well, did you all sing anything like ah, ah Swing Low Sweet Chariot and ah—
Mr. George Johnson: Yeah, we sing that too. We sing that too.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Did, di, di, did you si, si, did you sing that in your church, or did you learn that—
Mr. George Johnson: Sing that in church.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: —from outside?
Mr. George Johnson: Sing that in church.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Mhmm.

Mr. George Johnson: Sing that in church. Right in the church. Right down in church at home old Bethel Church. Sing it with our pastor, O. A. Douglass. Lil,[little] [pastor (?)] about my size but your color.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Well, wh, wh, where there, where there any songs like these spiritual and jubilee songs that they don't sing anymore, that they used to sing when you were, a long time ago?
Mr. George Johnson: Well, these special songs. They sing them in the revival, you understand. You see.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Mhmm.
Mr. George Johnson: Those special songs they sing in the revival. But after the revival, why, they [we had (?)] something else, you know.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Mhmm.
Mr. George Johnson: Yes, sir.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Well ah, do you remember what you favorite revival song was?

Mr. George Johnson: Well, I never had no favorite, just the ah older fellows had the, you know favorites, you understand. Like my uncle and all them old folks, you understand. They was leading the young folks, you understand.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Mhmm.
Mr. George Johnson: They'd take they message, you understand, and we'd go behind them, you know. You see. Let them lead us and we, we follow.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Did ah, did your uncle have a song that ah, everybody thought they really liked to hear him sing?
Mr. George Johnson: No. He never sing it. He, he always sung, he sang the same song about Me and My God [To Be (?)], all he sing.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Is that all?
Mr. George Johnson: Yes, sir. All he sing. He liked it.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Mhmm.
Mr. George Johnson: My uncle.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: But, but he, he didn't have one of the jubilees ah—
Mr. George Johnson: No, sir. No, sir. No, sir.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Nothing like that he liked.
Mr. George Johnson: No, sir. Nothing like that. He only sing, Me and My God [To Be (?)]. I heard him, he sung it all the time. [Wonderful (?)] fellow too.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Well where there any famous fiddlers around here when you came?
Mr. George Johnson: Fiddlers? Let me see. We had a, we had a fellow here [he ponders question] man, you ask me about a fiddler?
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Mhmm.

Mr. George Johnson: We had it after I was a boy down home. We had a fiddler down home there. We had a fiddler down home there named, Ed Phillips. He'd play that fiddle all night. Had a man pick a banjo, name ah, name Old Man Ed Green. And ah I think about a piece they used, used to play. He'd sing a song, you understand, his song but for his piece he used to play, you understand, say:

I Lost my fiddle and lost my bow.
Am glad I don't have go home and play no more.
[both men erupt in laughter]

And he had a cornstalk fiddle and a cornstalk bow. And never play no mo [more]. And he'd sing that song and play them fiddle and that banjo without end. Man name, Ed Phillips. Never forget his name. He lived right on the lake right across from Mound Brierfield Place. Right across, about three mile.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Mhmm.

Mr. George Johnson: [Somewhere (?)] by it over there at Lickfield Place, you understand. All that belonged to master Jeff, understand. That's his. All that land. And ah, they come over there and hear them cords and they'd play all night. They play all night just dance [like] three little old boys. Yes, sir.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Well, do you remember anything else they played besides from, I Lost My Fiddle and I Lost My Bow?
Mr. George Johnson: No. Naw, I'm a have to think about it. [long pause as he ponders question]
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Well did, well, did ah the children around the quarters have any games that they liked to play? That they sang to?
Mr. George Johnson: No. They, they always played ball and played marbles. And played [monpeg (?)].
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Mhmm.
Mr. George Johnson: See them chase it's night, you understand; see them going play [monpeg (?)], you understand. And they playing marbles. And playing baseball. They had no other games play.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: But, but little children didn't play any jumping games—
Mr. George Johnson: No, sir.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: —and singing games?

Mr. George Johnson: Nothing like that. No, sir. No, sir. We ain't had nothing like that. Then what we learned, you understand, we learned from children from Vicksburg. Children from Vicksburg, come down here excursions, you understand. Changed our children how to do things, you understand.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Mhmm.
Mr. George Johnson: They learned how to play croquette, so on like that. And learned them how to play dominoes.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Mhmm.

Mr. George Johnson: Showed them everything I was a boy. The children from Vicksburg come there on steamboats. They take our children, they all get in a gang, they all in there playing dominoes. Playing croquette and all like that, you know.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: They used to come, they used to come on excursions from Vicksburg—
Mr. George Johnson: Yes, sir.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: —to Davis Bend?

Mr. George Johnson: Davis Bend. The white people come down there in their hacks on steamboats just to see master Jeff's plantation, you understand. And drive them hacks all around, all the plantations see them niggas farm.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Mhmm.
Mr. George Johnson: On master Jeff's place. All the plantations.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: And to bring some of the colored people out—

Mr. George Johnson: Yes, sir. From the river. And they, people come up there all the way from Natchez up to Bend. Do the same thing. Come all around on the Bend and see mater Jeff's plan[tation]. Everybody come to see. Everybody.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Well—
Mr. George Johnson: Really why they come see master Jeff's folks.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Did they ever have celebrations like Cotton Pickings and celebrations at Christmas time?

Mr. George Johnson: Oh, yes, yes, lord, have mercy. We, we, now they wouldn't just have, they, they'd have Cotton Pickings. They'd have Cotton Picking;. They'd kill two, three hogs. And ah chop it up, you understand. Cook it. And have folks picking cotton. Some pick cotton at night. Moon shine at night. Pick cotton, understand. And they'd have a celeb[ration] for them in ???, ten, eleven o'clock come they'd have celebration for them. Cook this meat in a big wash pot. Cook it all night. And they all have a big time and after they get through picking cotton, they would ah eat, you understand. And after the, that time there was day they danced.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Mhmm.
Mr. George Johnson: They'd go in the house, they'd be in the house, and they'd dance, you understand. Dance for the day. That's right. No trouble at all.
Dr. Charles S. Johnson: Ah,did your ma—
